name: Zero-risk bias
statement: People prefer removing one source of harm completely to a larger cut in total harm, and pay a premium for the last unit of risk.
meaning: The test needs at least two sources of harm and a budget that cannot cover both. One option clears the smaller source and leaves the larger one nearly intact. Another cuts the total by more and leaves both in place. Taking the first is the bias. A second version shows up in what people will pay. The money attached to the final step, from a small risk down to none, exceeds what a step of the same size is worth anywhere else on the scale. Economists call that a certainty premium. Both versions rest on the same idea about attention: the label "safe" is easier to carry than a number, and a category that has been cleared needs no further thought. Neither version requires anyone to misread the figures. The choice can be made by someone who has the arithmetic in front of them.

origin.who: Jonathan Baron, Rajeev Gowda and Howard Kunreuther
origin.note: The paper mailed abstract, simplified liability cases to legislators, judges, oil and chemical executives, environmentalists and economists. Its abstract states that "A bias was found toward complete clean-up of some sites, or 'zero risk.'" The full text was not obtained. Wiley answers with a Cloudflare challenge rather than a paywall, Baron's own Pennsylvania pages return a bare 403 to every user agent tried, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar each record no open copy. Checked 21 September 2026. The abstract at Crossref is therefore all this page rests on for the origin. The behaviour predates the name. Viscusi, Magat and Huber reported certainty premiums in 1987, and Tversky and Kahneman set out the reasoning in 1981.

evidence: Tversky and Kahneman derived the prediction from the shape of the probability weighting function. An action that cuts the chance of a harm from one per cent to zero, they write, will be valued above one that cuts the same harm from two per cent to one. They note the same pattern in insurance: probabilistic cover that halves the chance of a loss is judged to be worth less than half the price of cover that removes the risk. Their note for that points to Kahneman and Tversky's own 1979 paper in Econometrica. They then report an unpublished study by Slovic, Fischhoff and Lichtenstein in which a vaccine cutting the chance of a disease from .20 to .10 was less attractive when described as effective in half of cases than when described as fully effective against one of two equally likely virus strains. No sample size and no percentages accompany it. Viscusi, Magat and Huber put risk-dollar tradeoffs to a sample of over 1,500 consumers over the risks of using an insecticide and a toilet bowl cleaner. Every subject started from 15 injuries per 10,000 bottles on each of two risks and priced six changes. Among subjects with young children, cutting both insecticide risks by a third was worth $1.84 on average, the next third $0.54, and the last third $5.71. Clearing both risks outright drew $8.09, against $2.38 for cutting each by two-thirds. Their abstract reports diminishing valuation as a reduction grows, certainty premiums for the total elimination of one risk, and no strong evidence of further premiums for eliminating several at once. Three of the four additivity tests pointed towards subadditivity and none reached significance at 5 per cent. Increases in risk were valued much more greatly than decreases. Cantarelli, Belle and Belardinelli describe the same study as finding parents willing to pay $2.38 more to cut two insecticide risks by two-thirds and $8.09 to remove them, and their description matches the paper's own table.

replication.headline: Where the design has been repeated the zero-risk option took 29 per cent of Italian nursing staff, then 90.7 per cent of 54 formulary directors in one scenario and 32.1 per cent of 53 in the next.
replication.detail: Cantarelli, Belle and Belardinelli built their test on Baron and colleagues and put it to the nursing staff of an Italian local health authority, 602 respondents at a 34 per cent response rate. Two developing countries have been hit by an infectious disease and vaccine doses are limited. One plan cuts deaths from 8,000 to 4,000 in one country and from 4,000 to 2,000 in the other. The other cuts deaths from 8,000 to 7,000 in one and from 4,000 to zero in the other. The paper prints 353 for the plan saving more lives and 142, or 29 per cent, for the plan that cleared one country, and gives no total for the item. Prosocial motivation was marginally higher among those choosing the larger saving, p = .010, and the two groups matched on age, sex, subordinates and job duties. Mezzio, Nguyen, Kiselica and O'Day sent their survey in October 2016 to a managed care network panel and got 54 replies to 76 invitations. In the first scenario, Drug A left no patients withdrawing for serious adverse events against seven on standard therapy, while Drug B left nine against 24. Drug B avoids more withdrawals, and 49 of the 54, or 90.7 per cent, chose Drug A, chi-square 35.85, P < 0.001. In the second, Drug C carried 6 cases of one adverse event and 34 of another, Drug D carried 12 and 42, and Drug E carried none of the first and 47 of the second. One reply naming Drug D was dropped as unrelated to the bias, leaving 53. There 67.9 per cent took Drug C and 32.1 per cent took the zero-risk Drug E, and the authors read the test as the sample moving away from the zero-risk choice, chi-square 6.81, P < 0.01. Their published conclusion is that there were no significant conclusions for zero-risk biases. Schneider, Streicher, Lermer, Sachs and Frey ran four studies across questionnaires and behavioural tasks, forced choice and free allocation of resources, and several decision domains. Their abstract reports the bias persistent over different methods and sensitive to context. It appeared more often in abstract tasks than concrete ones, a participant's zero-risk choices did not correlate between tasks, and the strategy looked appropriate when risks were divided over lottery urns but not when they were divided over people, where fairness entered the choice. Their full text was not obtained.

study.cite: Cantarelli, P., Belle, N., & Belardinelli, P. (2020). Behavioral public HR: Experimental evidence on cognitive biases and debiasing interventions. Review of Public Personnel Administration, 40(1), 56-81.

limits: No preregistered replication was located. The search covered Crossref, PubMed, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar's citation graph for both Baron and colleagues and Schneider and colleagues, and web searches aimed at OSF and PsyArXiv. Nothing preregistered, multi-site or adversarial came back. Checked 21 September 2026. Two of the three papers the idea rests on stayed closed. Wiley returns a Cloudflare challenge for Baron and colleagues, Hogrefe returns one for Schneider and colleagues to both a browser-like and a plain user agent, and Munich's repository holds a record for Schneider with no file attached. Viscusi, Magat and Huber was read in full from the version of record deposited in Vanderbilt's institutional repository, which Unpaywall and OpenAlex both record as closed. Both repeats used working professionals rather than the public, one Italian nursing staff and one American panel of 54. A sample that size cannot separate a real difference between two scenarios from noise, and the second scenario was analysed on 53 after one reply was dropped. Cantarelli and colleagues test their 29 per cent against an expected proportion of zero, which is a test that no non-empty result can fail, so the figure shows the choice exists and not that it is common. Schneider and colleagues report that a participant's choices did not correlate across their tasks, which leaves open whether there is a stable disposition to measure at all. Every figure on this page comes from a hypothetical scenario. No field data on real cleanup, procurement or formulary decisions was examined here.
misreadings: The waste-site item everybody quotes is not quoted from the paper. Descriptions circulating on the open web give two sites causing eight and four cancer cases a year, three cleanup plans, and 42 per cent of respondents ranking the worst plan above at least one other. Mezzio and colleagues carry a version of that figure, reporting 408 respondents and 42 per cent showing a bias towards the zero-risk option. That is a second-hand description rather than the paper, and the abstract states neither number. What is recorded above is only what the abstract states. The vaccine demonstration is credited to the wrong authors. Tversky and Kahneman describe it as an unpublished study by Slovic, Fischhoff and Lichtenstein and give no figures with it. The certainty effect, at no. 185, is a different claim. It concerns a single gamble whose probability is moved to one, and it is tested by comparing two pairs of prospects. Zero-risk bias concerns how a fixed effort is divided across two or more sources of harm, and it can be shown with no probabilities in the problem, as Mezzio and colleagues did with counts of patients. Probability neglect, at no. 191, is a third claim again, and the phrase is Cass Sunstein's. Rottenstreich and Hsee's own prediction is that the weighting function is more S-shaped for outcomes carrying strong feeling, so people are more sensitive to departures from impossibility and from certainty and less sensitive to variation in between. Someone who reads the numbers correctly and still clears the smaller site is showing zero-risk bias while neglecting nothing. The certainty premium does not stack. Viscusi, Magat and Huber found premiums for eliminating one risk and no strong evidence of extra premiums for eliminating several. Calling the choice irrational assumes total harm is the only thing being weighed. Schneider and colleagues found that dividing risk over people brought fairness into the decision in a way that dividing it over lottery urns did not. In both repeats that followed Baron's design closely, the zero-risk option was the minority answer.
